title: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
summary: Learn the Python a security job needs: text and bytes, regex log parsing, CSV and JSON, file hashing, encodings, safe API calls with rate limits, a command-line tool, safe habits and tests.
outcomes: Explain the difference between text and bytes and decode hostile log data without crashing or losing evidence
Write a regex that counts failed SSH logins per address and spot credential stuffing in the result
Parse CSV exports and JSON records with the standard library and flag rows that match published indicators
Hash files in chunks and check them against normalized known-bad lists, knowing what a miss does not prove
Decode base64, hex and URL encoding, and explain why detections must normalize input before matching
Call a threat-intel API with timeouts, keys from the environment, input validation, rate limiting and caching
Package a script as an argparse tool with exit codes, avoid eval and shell=True, and test it offline with pytest

lessons.title: Why security teams script, and your first Python program

blocks.md:
Most security work is reading data that someone else's software wrote: log lines, alert records, lists of suspicious file hashes, answers from web services. A person can read fifty lines by eye. Nobody can read fifty thousand. A **script** (a short program that does a job you would otherwise do by hand) reads all of them the same careful way, every time.

This is why employers ask for it. A DevDump scan of 100 live security job postings in November 2026 found Python named in 57 of them, more than any security product or certification, and "security automation or scripting" listed as a requirement in almost every role family, from SOC (security operations center) analysts to cloud and application security engineers.

**Python** is a programming language created by Guido van Rossum. The name has nothing to do with snakes: the [Python FAQ](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/general.html) says van Rossum was reading scripts of *Monty Python's Flying Circus*, a 1970s BBC comedy series, and wanted a name that was short, unique and slightly mysterious.

You write Python in a plain text file ending in `.py` and run it by typing `python3 script.py` in a terminal (the window where you type commands). The **interpreter** (the program called `python3`) first checks the whole file and translates it into an internal form called bytecode, then carries out each line in order. There is no separate build step, so you can change a line and run it again in a second.

Here is the whole vocabulary for your first script:

- A **variable** is a name for a value. `failed = 0` makes the name `failed` point at the number 0.
- A **string** is a piece of text in quotes, like `"Failed password"`.
- A **list** is an ordered collection in square brackets, like `["a", "b"]`.
- `for line in lines:` runs the indented block once per item, with `line` set to that item.
- `if condition:` runs its indented block only when the condition is true.

Indentation (the spaces at the start of a line) is not decoration in Python: it is how the interpreter knows which lines belong inside the loop or the `if`.

blocks.code:
lines = [
    "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 52144 ssh2",
    "Accepted password for alice from 198.51.100.4 port 40022 ssh2",
    "Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.7 port 52150 ssh2",
    "Failed password for invalid user test from 192.0.2.55 port 61001 ssh2",
    "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 52161 ssh2",
]
failed = 0
for line in lines:
    if line.startswith("Failed"):
        failed = failed + 1
print("failed logins:", failed)
blocks.caption: count_failed.py: five lines in the format the OpenSSH server writes (addresses are from the ranges reserved for documentation). Output: `failed logins: 4`

blocks.title: The loop visits each log line once
blocks.code:
lines = [
    "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 52144 ssh2",
    "Accepted password for alice from 198.51.100.4 port 40022 ssh2",
    "Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.7 port 52150 ssh2",
    "Failed password for invalid user test from 192.0.2.55 port 61001 ssh2",
    "Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 52161 ssh2",
]
failed = 0
for line in lines:
    if line.startswith("Failed"):
        failed = failed + 1
print("failed logins:", failed)

scenes.caption: Lines 1 to 7 build a list of five strings. Nothing is counted yet; the list just sits in memory under the name lines.
The counter starts at zero. Every script that counts things starts this way.
First pass of the loop: line now holds the first string. startswith checks only the beginning of the text.
The condition was true, so the indented line runs and the counter goes up by one.
Second pass: an Accepted line. startswith("Failed") is false, so the counter line is skipped.
Passes three to five are all Failed lines, so the counter reaches 4. Then the list is used up and the loop ends.
Back at the left margin, print runs once and shows the result.

blocks.prompt: A real log file often has a timestamp and host name before the message, like `Nov 13 09:14:02 web1 sshd[2301]: Failed password ...`. What does the script above count on such lines?
blocks.reveal: Zero. `startswith("Failed")` looks only at the very first characters, and those are now `Nov 13`. The script still runs without any error and confidently prints the wrong number. This is the most common way security scripts fail: not with a crash but with a silent miscount. The rest of the course builds the habits that catch it: parse the exact field you mean (lesson 5) and write tests with realistic input (lesson 13).

blocks.md:
Strings come with **methods** (functions attached to a value, called with a dot). The ones you will use constantly:

- `s.strip()` removes spaces and the newline from both ends.
- `s.split()` cuts the text at runs of whitespace and returns a list of words.
- `s.lower()` returns a lowercase copy, for case-insensitive checks.
- `x in s` is true when the text `x` appears anywhere in `s`.

List positions start at 0, and negative positions count from the end, so `words[-1]` is the last word. An **f-string** (a string with `f` before the quote) fills in the values of names written in curly braces.

blocks.code:
line = "  Failed password for root from 203.0.113.7 port 52144 ssh2\n"
clean = line.strip()
words = clean.split()
print(words[0], words[-1], len(words))
print(words[5])
print(f"user={words[3]} ip={words[5]}")
print("ROOT" in clean, "root" in clean.lower())
blocks.caption: Output: `Failed ssh2 9` / `203.0.113.7` / `user=root ip=203.0.113.7` / `False True`

blocks.title: split() turns one log line into numbered words

scenes.caption: After strip and split, the line is a list of 9 words (shown shortened to fit). Each word has a position number starting at 0.
words[0] is the first word and words[-1] is the last. Negative positions count back from the end.
words[3] is the user and words[5] is the address 203.0.113.7. This works only while every line has exactly this shape, which is why lesson 5 replaces it with a pattern.

blocks.md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

blocks.question: Line 10 of count_failed.py is changed to `if "failed" in line:`. What does the script print for the same five lines?
options: failed logins: 4
failed logins: 5
An error, because in only works on lists
failed logins: 0
blocks.explain: `in` is case-sensitive. The lines contain `Failed` with a capital F, never `failed`, so nothing matches and the count is 0. Use `"failed" in line.lower()` when you want a case-insensitive check. `in` works on strings as well as lists.

lessons.title: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores

blocks.md:
Everything a computer stores or sends is a sequence of **bytes**: numbers from 0 to 255, each made of 8 bits. Text is an idea on top of that. To store the word `café` you need a rule that maps each character to bytes. That rule is an **encoding**.

The oldest common one is **ASCII** (American Standard Code for Information Interchange), which covers 128 characters: English letters, digits and punctuation, one byte each. It has no `é`, no Arabic, no emoji.

**Unicode** gives every character in every script a number called a **code point**: `A` is 65 and `é` is 233. **UTF-8** (a Unicode transformation format that works in 8-bit units, defined in [RFC 3629](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629.txt)) turns code points into 1 to 4 bytes. ASCII characters stay one byte, identical to ASCII, which is why UTF-8 became the default for files and the web.

Python keeps the two ideas apart with two types:

- `str` is text: a sequence of characters. Written `"café"`.
- `bytes` is raw data: a sequence of numbers 0 to 255. Written `b"caf"`.

`.encode("utf-8")` turns text into bytes and `.decode("utf-8")` turns bytes back into text.

blocks.code:
name = "café"
data = name.encode("utf-8")
print(len(name), len(data))
print(data)
print(data.hex(" "))
print(data.decode("utf-8"))
raw = b"user=\xff\xfeadmin"
print(raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
blocks.caption: Output: `4 5` / `b'caf\xc3\xa9'` / `63 61 66 c3 a9` / `café` / `user=��admin`

blocks.title: Four characters become five bytes

scenes.caption: The string has 4 characters, so len(name) is 4. The encoded bytes are shown in hex (base 16, digits 0 to 9 then a to f, two digits per byte).
c, a and f are ASCII, so UTF-8 stores each as one byte: 63, 61, 66 in hex, the same values ASCII uses.
é (code point 233) is outside ASCII, so UTF-8 spends two bytes on it: c3 a9. That is why len(data) is 5, not 4.
Decoding reverses it: the decoder sees c3, knows a two-byte character starts, reads a9 and rebuilds é.

blocks.md:
Why a security engineer cares:

- **Hashes need bytes.** A hash (lesson 7) is a fixed-size fingerprint of some data, and `hashlib.sha256("abc")` raises `TypeError: Strings must be encoded before hashing`. You hash `"abc".encode("utf-8")`, and a different encoding gives a different hash.
- **Attackers control bytes, not just text.** A log line can contain bytes that are not valid UTF-8. `b"\xff".decode("utf-8")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` and stops your script halfway through a log. `errors="replace"` swaps bad bytes for the replacement character � and keeps going, so one hostile line cannot kill your whole run.
- **Same look, different bytes.** `é` can be one code point or `e` followed by a combining accent. They print the same but encode to `c3 a9` versus `65 cc 81`, so they compare unequal and hash differently. `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)` folds them to one form, as the [Unicode HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html) explains.

Do not "fix" decode errors with `errors="ignore"` in security tooling. It silently deletes the bad bytes, so `ad\xffmin` becomes `admin` and your report shows a username the attacker never sent. Prefer `replace`, which leaves a visible mark.

blocks.prompt: You read a file with `open(path)` and no encoding argument, on a laptop and then on an older Windows server. Could the same file decode differently?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The [open() docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html) say the default became UTF-8 only in Python 3.15. On older versions, or when UTF-8 Mode is switched off, the default is whatever encoding the platform's locale reports, which differs between systems. The same bytes can then become different text, or fail to decode on one machine only. Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` (and usually `errors="replace"`) when reading logs, so the script behaves the same on every machine and Python version it runs on.

blocks.md: Text is characters, bytes are numbers. Decode at the edge of your program (when you read), work with `str` inside, and encode again only when you hash, send or write bytes.

blocks.question: What does `len("é".encode("utf-8"))` return?
options: It raises an error because é is not ASCII
blocks.explain: `é` is code point 233, above the ASCII range, so UTF-8 encodes it as two bytes (c3 a9). `len` of the string itself would be 1.

blocks.question: A script decodes each log line with `errors="strict"` (the default). One line in a million contains the byte 0xff. What happens?
options: That line is skipped automatically
The byte becomes a question mark
A UnicodeDecodeError stops the script unless you catch it
Python guesses another encoding for that line
blocks.explain: Strict decoding raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on invalid bytes. Unless you catch it (lesson 4) or use `errors="replace"`, the run ends at that line and the rest of the log is never checked.

lessons.title: Lists, dictionaries and sets: counting what matters

blocks.md:
Most security questions are counting questions. Which address failed to log in most often? How many distinct users did it try? Which hashes appear more than once? Python has three containers that answer them:

- A **list** keeps items in order and allows repeats: `["a", "b", "a"]`.
- A **dict** (short for dictionary: like a real dictionary, it maps a key to a value, the way a word maps to its definition) is written `{"203.0.113.7": 3}`. Looking up a key is fast no matter how many keys there are.
- A **set** holds unique items with no order: `{"a", "b"}`. Adding something already inside does nothing.
The classic counting pattern uses a dict. For each item, read its current count with `counts.get(ip, 0)` (the `0` is the default when the key is not there yet), add one, and store it back.

blocks.code:
ips = ["203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55", "203.0.113.7",
       "198.51.100.4", "203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55"]

counts = {}
for ip in ips:
    counts[ip] = counts.get(ip, 0) + 1
print(counts)

noisy = [ip for ip, n in counts.items() if n >= 2]
print(noisy)
print(sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)[0])
blocks.caption: Output: `{'203.0.113.7': 3, '192.0.2.55': 2, '198.51.100.4': 1}` / `['203.0.113.7', '192.0.2.55']` / `203.0.113.7`

blocks.title: Building a count per address, one item at a time
blocks.code:
ips = ["203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55", "203.0.113.7",
       "198.51.100.4", "203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55"]

counts = {}
for ip in ips:
    counts[ip] = counts.get(ip, 0) + 1
print(counts)

noisy = [ip for ip, n in counts.items() if n >= 2]
print(noisy)
print(sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)[0])

scenes.caption: Six addresses, as a failed-login parser might extract them. counts starts as an empty dict.
First item: get returns the default 0 because the key is new, plus one gives 1.
Second item is a new address, so it also starts at 1.
Third item repeats the first address. get now returns 1, so its count becomes 2.
After all six: 3, 2 and 1. A dict keeps keys in the order they were first added.
A list comprehension builds a new list in one line: every ip whose count n is at least 2.
sorted with key=counts.get orders addresses by their count; reverse=True puts the biggest first.

blocks.md:
The line `[ip for ip, n in counts.items() if n >= 2]` is a **list comprehension**: read it as "the list of `ip`, for each `ip, n` pair in the dict, keeping those where `n >= 2`". `counts.items()` gives the dict's key and value together.

Counting is so common that the standard library has a ready-made tool: `collections.Counter` from the [collections module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html), a dict that counts for you and can list the most common items.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter

ips = ["203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55", "203.0.113.7",
       "198.51.100.4", "203.0.113.7", "192.0.2.55"]
counts = Counter(ips)
print(counts.most_common(2))
print(counts["10.9.9.9"])
seen = set(ips)
print(len(ips), len(seen))
blocks.caption: Output: `[('203.0.113.7', 3), ('192.0.2.55', 2)]` / `0` / `6 3`

blocks.title: The same counts as a chart

scenes.caption: Counter(ips) holds exactly what the hand-written loop built. most_common(2) returns the two tallest bars as (address, count) pairs.

blocks.md: A `Counter` returns 0 for a key it has never seen, instead of raising `KeyError` like a plain dict. That makes `counts[ip] += 1` safe on the first sighting, and `counts["10.9.9.9"]` above prints 0.

Sets answer "how many distinct" questions. `len(set(ips))` is the number of different addresses. Later you will keep a set of usernames per address: one address trying many different usernames is the signature of **credential stuffing** (trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites), while one address trying one username many times looks like password guessing. Sets also make lookups against a list of known-bad indicators fast: `ip in bad_ips` costs the same for ten entries or ten million.

blocks.question: You want to know whether an address appears in a list of 2 million known-bad addresses, checked once per log line. Which container should hold the bad addresses?
options: A list, because it keeps the order from the threat feed
A set, because membership checks do not slow down as it grows
A string with all addresses joined by commas
A list sorted alphabetically
blocks.explain: `x in some_list` compares against items one by one, so it gets slower as the list grows. A set (like dict keys) uses hashing to jump straight to the right slot. A joined string can also give false matches: `1.2.3.4` is inside `11.2.3.45`.

lessons.title: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input

blocks.md:
Real data lives in files, and files go missing, have the wrong permissions or contain junk. This lesson adds three tools that turn a demo into something you can run on a server at 3 a.m.

A **function** is a named, reusable block of code. `def read_lines(path):` defines one that takes a **parameter** called `path`; `return` hands a value back to whoever called it. Functions let you test one piece at a time and reuse it in every script.

`open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` opens a file for reading text. The `with` statement closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if something goes wrong inside it. Looping over an open file gives you one line at a time, so a 10 GB log never has to fit in memory.

An **exception** is Python's way of reporting that something went wrong: a missing file raises `FileNotFoundError`, turning `"ssh2"` into a number raises `ValueError`. Uncaught, an exception stops the program and prints a traceback. `try:` ... `except SomeError:` catches a specific kind and lets you decide what to do.

blocks.code:
def read_lines(path):
    """Return the lines of a text file, or [] if it is missing."""
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
            return [line.rstrip("\n") for line in f]
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"warning: {path} not found")
        return []

lines = read_lines("auth.log")
print(len(lines))
print(lines[0][:32])
print(read_lines("missing.log"))
blocks.caption: Output, using the 13-line sample auth.log printed in full in lesson 5 (save it next to the script first): `13` / `Nov 13 09:14:02 web1 sshd[2301]:` / `warning: missing.log not found` / `[]`

blocks.title: Two calls: the happy path and the missing file
blocks.code:
def read_lines(path):
    """Return the lines of a text file, or [] if it is missing."""
    try:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
            return [line.rstrip("\n") for line in f]
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"warning: {path} not found")
        return []

lines = read_lines("auth.log")
print(len(lines))
print(lines[0][:32])
print(read_lines("missing.log"))

scenes.caption: Defining the function runs nothing yet. Python just remembers the name read_lines and its body.
First call with auth.log. Execution jumps into the function with path set to that name and enters the try block.
The file opens. The comprehension reads every line and strips the trailing newline from each.
Back outside, len(lines) is 13, and slicing [:32] shows the first 32 characters of line one.
Second call with a file that does not exist. open raises FileNotFoundError and the rest of the try block is skipped.
The matching except block runs instead: it warns and returns an empty list, so the caller keeps going.
scenes.output:
13
Nov 13 09:14:02 web1 sshd[2301]:
warning: missing.log not found
[]

blocks.md: The text in triple quotes right under `def` is a **docstring**: documentation that tools and `help(read_lines)` can show. The same pattern guards conversions of untrusted fields:

blocks.caption: Output: `52144 None`

blocks.md: Never write a bare `except:` or `except Exception: pass` around a whole script. It also swallows bugs in your own code and even Ctrl+C in the bare form, so the script reports "no alerts" when it actually crashed on line 2. Catch the specific exception you expect, at the place you can handle it, and let everything else fail loudly.

blocks.prompt: Should `read_lines` return `[]` for a missing file, or let the exception reach the caller?
blocks.reveal: It depends on what the caller needs, and that is a design decision you should make on purpose. For a convenience script that scans many optional files, a warning and an empty list is fine. For a detection job, an empty result looks exactly like "no attacks found", which is the worst possible silent failure. There the better choice is to let the error surface (or exit with a non-zero code, lesson 11) so someone notices the log went missing. Attackers delete logs precisely because missing data is so often read as good news.

blocks.md: Read files with `with open(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")`, put reusable steps in functions, and catch only the exceptions you can handle. A missing log is a finding, not a zero.

blocks.question: Which line correctly opens a log so that one invalid byte cannot stop the script?
options: open(path)
open(path, "rb")
open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
open(path, encoding="ascii")
blocks.explain: With `errors="replace"` invalid bytes become the replacement character and reading continues. `"rb"` would avoid decoding entirely but then every line is `bytes`, not text, and string methods with `str` arguments fail. ASCII would reject any non-ASCII byte.

lessons.title: Regular expressions: counting failed logins per address

blocks.md: Splitting on spaces broke as soon as the line shape changed. A **regular expression** (regex for short) is a small pattern language for describing text: "the word Failed, then anything without spaces, then the word from, then an address". The notation began as a simple model of computation studied by theorists; as Russ Cox's article [Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast](https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html) recounts, Ken Thompson (later a co-creator of Unix) brought it to programmers in the QED text editor. Python's version lives in the `re` module.

The pieces you need for log parsing:

- Ordinary characters match themselves: `port` matches the text port.
- `\d` is one digit (in Python it also matches digits from other scripts, such as Arabic-Indic; write `[0-9]` when only 0 to 9 should count), `\S` is one non-space character, and `+` means one or more of the thing before it. So `\d+` is a number and `\S+` is a word.
- `(?:invalid user )?` is a group that may appear zero or one time.
- `(?P<ip>...)` is a **named group**: whatever it matches is saved under the name `ip`, so you can read `m["ip"]` later.

Write patterns as raw strings, `r"..."`. In a normal string Python itself would try to interpret the backslashes before `re` ever sees them; the [re docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html) recommend raw strings for exactly this reason.

The pattern must match what the program really writes, so read the source rather than guessing. In OpenSSH's [auth.c](https://github.com/openssh/openssh-portable/blob/master/auth.c) the server logs every password attempt as `Failed password for USER from ADDRESS port N ssh2` (or `Accepted ...`), inserting `invalid user ` before the name when the account does not exist. It also writes a separate `Invalid user NAME from ADDRESS port N` line. Here is a small sample log, 13 lines, built in that format:
