Nov 13 09:16:00 web1 sshd[2320]: Accepted password for alice from 198.51.100.4 port 40022 ssh2
Nov 13 09:16:30 web1 sshd[2321]: Failed password for alice from 2001:db8::5 port 40100 ssh2
blocks.caption: auth.log (sample data; addresses from ranges reserved for documentation)

blocks.code:
import re
from collections import Counter

FAILED = re.compile(
    r"Failed password for (?:invalid user )?(?P<user>\S+) "
    r"from (?P<ip>\S+) port (?P<port>\d+) ssh2"
)

def failed_by_ip(lines):
    counts = Counter()
    users = {}
    for line in lines:
        m = FAILED.search(line)
        if m is None:
            continue
        ip = m["ip"]
        counts[ip] += 1
        users.setdefault(ip, set()).add(m["user"])
    return counts, users

with open("auth.log", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
    counts, users = failed_by_ip(f)

for ip, n in counts.most_common():
    print(f"{ip:<14} failures={n} users={len(users[ip])}")
blocks.caption: Output: `203.0.113.7    failures=5 users=5` / `192.0.2.55     failures=3 users=1` / `2001:db8::5    failures=1 users=1`

blocks.title: How the pattern walks one log line

scenes.caption: Line 5 of auth.log, cut into words for display (pw is password, IP is 203.0.113.7). search() scans for the first place the whole pattern fits; the timestamp before it is skipped.
The literal text Failed password for must match exactly. It does.
The optional group for invalid user matches here. On a line for a real account it would match nothing and the pattern would still go on.
The named group user grabs the next run of non-space characters and saves it under that name.
After the literal from, the named group ip saves the address. Because it accepts any non-space characters, an IPv6 address such as 2001:db8::5 works too.
port, then the digits-only group port saves 52144, then the literal ssh2. The whole pattern fit, so search returns a match object.

blocks.title: Matching the word from versus matching the full message

scenes.caption: A lazy shortcut, counting every from ADDRESS in the file, gives these numbers. 203.0.113.7 gets 8.
The full Failed password pattern gives 5, 3, 0, 1. The shortcut also counted 2 Invalid user lines and 1 successful login, and it blamed a user who logged in normally.

blocks.md: Now read the result like an analyst. 192.0.2.55 tried one account, `root`, three times: password guessing. 203.0.113.7 tried five different accounts once each, then logged in successfully as `deploy` one second later. That shape fits **credential stuffing** (from the log alone it could also be password spraying, one common password tried on many accounts), which the [OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Credential_stuffing) (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) community defines as the automated injection of stolen username and password pairs into login forms. It works because people reuse passwords, so a pair leaked from one site often opens another. MITRE ATT&CK, the public catalog of attacker techniques, lists it as [T1110.004](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/004/).

**Real case: Snowflake customers, 2024.** Mandiant, Google's incident response firm, [reported](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc5537-snowflake-data-theft-extortion/) that a group it tracks as UNC5537 ([UNC for uncategorized](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/how-mandiant-tracks-uncategorized-threat-actors/): a cluster not yet tied to a named actor) logged into customer accounts on Snowflake (a cloud data warehouse service) with credentials stolen by infostealer malware (programs that copy saved passwords off infected computers), some from infections as old as 2020. About 165 organizations were notified. The accounts had no multi-factor authentication (MFA), passwords had not been rotated for as long as four years, and no network allow lists limited where logins could come from. Mandiant's recommendations include alerting on abnormal access attempts, which is exactly what a script like this one starts to do.

A per-address threshold is easy to evade. Mandiant saw UNC5537 log in mostly through commercial VPN (virtual private network) addresses, and stuffing tools can spread attempts so each address fails only once or twice. Also count failures per username, and treat any success after failures as more important than the failures themselves.

blocks.question: You use the pattern `r"\d+"` with `re.findall` to pull the port number out of `port 52144 ssh2`. What comes back?
blocks.explain: findall returns every non-overlapping match, and the 2 in ssh2 is also a run of digits. This is why the course pattern anchors the number between the literal words port and ssh2: context makes a pattern match only the field you mean.

blocks.question: Which log shape most strongly suggests credential stuffing rather than password guessing?
options: One address, one username, 300 failures
Many addresses, each failing once on the root account over a month
A single failed login at 3 a.m.
One address, 40 different usernames, one attempt each, then a success
blocks.explain: Stuffing replays known pairs: each account is tried about once, with whatever password leaked for it, and some succeed because of password reuse. Many attempts on one account is guessing. The success at the end is the urgent part: it means a working stolen credential.

lessons.title: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them

blocks.md:
Logs are not the only format you will meet. Two others are everywhere in security data:

- **CSV** (comma-separated values, documented in [RFC 4180](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4180.txt)): a table as text, one row per line, fields separated by commas. Spreadsheets, SIEM (security information and event management) exports and cloud audit downloads all use it.
- **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation, [RFC 8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt)): nested data as text, with objects in curly braces, lists in square brackets, strings in double quotes, numbers, `true`, `false` and `null`. Almost every web API answers in JSON.

Both look simple enough to split by hand. Both will bite you if you do.

**The case data.** Mandiant's Snowflake report printed two real login records left by UNC5537, including client addresses 37.19.210.21 and 45.27.26.205 and a client environment in JSON whose `APPLICATION` field read `DBeaver_DBeaverUltimate` (DBeaver is a database tool the group used). Snowflake keeps a [LOGIN_HISTORY](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/account-usage/login_history) view with the client address, the reported client type and the second authentication factor, which is empty when MFA was not used. The file below is a simplified export modeled on that, with the two published indicators planted in it:

blocks.code:
time,user,client_ip,client_env,mfa,success
2024-04-14 10:04:10,svc_report,37.19.210.21,"{""APPLICATION"": ""DBeaver_DBeaverUltimate"", ""OS"": ""Windows Server 2022""}",no,yes
2024-04-14 11:20:45,ana,198.51.100.4,"{""APPLICATION"": ""Snowflake UI"", ""OS"": ""macOS""}",yes,yes
2024-05-31 20:10:13,etl_bot,45.27.26.205,"{""APPLICATION"": ""PythonConnector"", ""OS"": ""Darwin""}",no,no
2024-05-31 20:11:02,etl_bot,198.51.100.20,"{""APPLICATION"": ""PythonConnector"", ""OS"": ""Linux""}",no,yes
blocks.caption: logins.csv (simplified sample; not a real customer's data)

blocks.prompt: Row two has a comma inside its JSON field. What does `line.split(",")` give you for that row?
blocks.reveal: Seven pieces instead of six. The JSON `{"APPLICATION": ..., "OS": ...}` contains a comma, so a plain split cuts it in half, and every field after it shifts one position: your `mfa` column now holds part of the JSON. CSV handles this by wrapping the field in double quotes and doubling any quote inside it (`""`), which is why the file looks so odd. Only a real CSV parser understands those rules.

blocks.title: split(",") versus csv.reader on the same row

scenes.caption: Naive split: 7 pieces. The quoted JSON field was cut at its internal comma, so the row has one field too many.
Every field after the cut is shifted. Code that reads position 4 as mfa now gets half a JSON object, and position 5, where code expects the success flag, now holds the mfa value.
csv.reader follows the quoting rules: 6 fields, the JSON intact in one of them, the doubled quotes turned back into single ones.

blocks.md:
`csv.DictReader` goes one step further: it reads the header row and gives you each row as a dict, so you write `row["client_ip"]` instead of remembering that the address is field 2. The [csv docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html) say to open the file with `newline=""` so the module, not Python's newline handling, deals with line endings inside quoted fields.

`json.loads(text)` turns JSON text into Python values: objects become dicts, arrays become lists, `true` becomes `True` and `null` becomes `None`. `json.dumps(value)` goes the other way. Use `.get("KEY")` on parsed data when a field may be missing: it returns `None` instead of raising `KeyError`.

blocks.caption: Output: `2024-04-14 10:04:10 svc_report ioc-ip,ioc-app,no-mfa` / `2024-05-31 20:10:13 etl_bot ioc-ip` / `2024-05-31 20:11:02 etl_bot no-mfa`

blocks.title: Each row collects reasons, then prints only if it has any

scenes.caption: Indicators are sets: the two client addresses and the client application name Mandiant published.
Row 1: DictReader gives a dict keyed by the header. The JSON field is parsed into its own dict.
All three checks fire: a listed address, a listed application, and a successful login with no second factor.
Row 2: ana used MFA from an unlisted address with the normal web UI. reasons stays empty, so nothing prints.
Row 3: a listed address, but the login failed, so only ioc-ip. Row 4: an unlisted address, but a successful login without MFA.
scenes.output:
2024-04-14 10:04:10 svc_report ioc-ip,ioc-app,no-mfa
2024-05-31 20:10:13 etl_bot ioc-ip
2024-05-31 20:11:02 etl_bot no-mfa

blocks.md: Treat client-reported fields as hints, not proof. Snowflake's documentation says the reported client type "is not authenticated": the connecting program says what it is, and an attacker can say anything. The application name `DBeaver_DBeaverUltimate` caught this campaign, but the next one will use a different name. The no-MFA check is about your own configuration and stays useful.

Invalid JSON raises `json.JSONDecodeError`, which is a kind of `ValueError`. A common surprise: Python's dict notation is not JSON. `json.loads("{'APPLICATION': 'x'}")` fails because JSON requires double quotes. When one malformed record should not stop a whole export, wrap the parse in `try`/`except json.JSONDecodeError` and count the bad rows so they show up in your report.

Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

blocks.question: A threat feed sends `{"ip": "45.27.26.205", "active": false, "score": null}`. After `d = json.loads(text)`, what is `d["score"]`?
options: The string "null"
None
It raises KeyError
blocks.explain: JSON `null` becomes Python `None`, and `false` becomes `False`. The key exists, so there is no KeyError; it simply holds no value. Check `if d["score"] is None` before doing arithmetic with it.

lessons.title: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists

blocks.md:
A **hash function** reads any amount of data and returns a short fixed-size fingerprint called a **digest**. Change one bit of the input and the digest changes completely; the same input always gives the same digest. That makes hashes the standard way to name a file in security work: an alert says "this SHA-256", not "the file called invoice.exe", because names are easy to change and contents are not.

Two families appear in every advisory:

- **MD5** (Message-Digest algorithm 5, [RFC 1321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1321.txt)): 128 bits, written as 32 hex digits.
- **SHA-256** (Secure Hash Algorithm with a 256-bit digest, from the US standard [FIPS 180-4](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)): 64 hex digits. SHA-1 (40 hex digits) sits between them.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

print(hashlib.sha256(b"abc").hexdigest())
print(hashlib.sha256(b"abd").hexdigest())
blocks.caption: Output: `ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad` / `a52d159f262b2c6ddb724a61840befc36eb30c88877a4030b65cbe86298449c9`. One letter changed, and the two digests share nothing visible.

blocks.md: To hash a file, open it in binary mode (`"rb"`, because hashing works on bytes) and feed it to the hash object in **chunks**, a fixed number of bytes at a time. A 4 GB disk image then needs only 64 KB of memory. `hashlib.new(name)` picks the algorithm by name; `update` adds bytes; `hexdigest` returns the result as hex text. Python 3.11 added [hashlib.file_digest](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html), which does the chunk loop for you, but writing it once shows what happens.

blocks.caption: Output (notes.txt contains the six bytes hello plus a newline): `5891b5b522d5df086d0ff0b110fbd9d21bb4fc7163af34d08286a2e846f6be03` / `b1946ac92492d2347c6235b4d2611184` / `False` / `False` / `True`

blocks.title: Hashing a 150 KB file in 64 KB chunks

scenes.caption: 153,600 bytes, read 65,536 at a time. Memory use stays at one chunk no matter how large the file is.
Each chunk goes into update. The hash object keeps a small internal state and forgets the chunk itself.
Second chunk, same thing. The digest depends on every byte in order, so chunk size does not change the answer.
The last chunk is short: 153,600 minus 131,072 is 22,528 bytes.
read returns empty bytes at end of file, which is falsy, so the loop breaks and hexdigest produces the final fingerprint.

blocks.md: **Real case: WannaCry, 2017.** WannaCry was ransomware that spread across networks through a flaw in SMB (Server Message Block, the Windows file-sharing protocol) that Microsoft had patched as MS17-010. US-CERT (the US Computer Emergency Readiness Team, whose alerts are now hosted by CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) published alert [TA17-132A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2017/05/12/indicators-associated-wannacry-ransomware) with tens of thousands of infections reported in over 150 countries. Its text names two MD5 digests: the dropper (the program that carries and installs the ransomware) as `5bef35496fcbdbe841c82f4d1ab8b7c2` and, inside a detection rule, `4DA1F312A214C07143ABEEAFB695D904`. Notice the second one is in capitals. Hashes like these are **IOCs** (indicators of compromise): observable facts that point to an intrusion.

blocks.prompt: Without the `.lower()` normalization line, would checking a file whose MD5 is the capitalized hash from the alert work?
blocks.reveal: No. `hexdigest()` always returns lowercase, and string comparison is exact, so `"4da1..." in KNOWN_BAD_MD5` is False even though it is the same hash. That is the fourth line of output above. Normalize every indicator when you load it (strip spaces, lowercase) and compare normalized values only. Feeds copied from PDFs and web pages are full of capital letters, trailing spaces and invisible characters.

blocks.md: **Real case: Codecov, 2021.** Codecov's Bash Uploader was a script that customers' CI (continuous integration) pipelines downloaded and ran during builds to upload test coverage reports. Codecov's [security update](https://about.codecov.io/security-update/) says that from January 31, 2021 an attacker periodically altered the hosted script so it sent environment variables from customers' CI runs to a third-party server. It was caught on April 1 when a customer compared the checksum (shasum) of the downloaded script with the one Codecov published on GitHub and saw they differed. Codecov noted that customers who did that checksum comparison before running the script may not have been affected. That check is the `hash_file` function plus one `==`.

A hash match is strong evidence; a hash miss proves nothing. Security researcher David Bianco's [Pyramid of Pain](https://detect-respond.blogspot.com/2013/03/the-pyramid-of-pain.html) puts hash values at the bottom because changing a single byte gives the attacker a brand new hash. Use hash lists to catch known copies quickly, never as the only control.

One more caution about algorithms. MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collision attacks: someone can craft two different files with the same digest. [RFC 6151](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6151.txt) says MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required, and the hashlib docs warn about both. They are still fine for looking up IOCs that advisories publish in MD5, but use SHA-256 when you are proving that a file was not tampered with, as in the Codecov check.
Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

blocks.question: You change one byte at the very end of a 2 GB file. How much of its SHA-256 digest changes?
options: About half of the bits, so it looks like a completely unrelated digest
Only the last hex digit or two
Nothing, because SHA-256 samples only the start of large files
The digest length grows by one byte
blocks.explain: Cryptographic hashes are designed so that any change to the input flips about half the output bits, unpredictably. The digest length is always fixed (64 hex digits for SHA-256), and every byte of the input counts.

blocks.question: Your script reports "0 matches" after hashing every file on a server against 20,000 SHA-256 IOCs from a vendor feed. What can you honestly conclude?
options: The server is clean
The feed must be broken
The attacker used MD5 instead
None of the files is an exact copy of a listed file
blocks.explain: Hash matching only detects byte-identical copies. Recompiled, repacked or slightly edited malware has a different hash, and so do files the feed never saw. Report what you actually tested.

lessons.title: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them

blocks.md:
An **encoding** in this sense rewrites bytes as different bytes so they survive a channel that only accepts certain characters. It is not encryption: there is no key, and anyone can reverse it. Three show up constantly:

- **Hex** (hexadecimal, base 16): each byte becomes two characters from 0 to 9 and a to f. `foo` is `666f6f`.
- **Base64**: named for its alphabet of 64 symbols (A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9, + and /), each carrying 6 bits, plus `=` for padding, as [RFC 4648](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt) defines. Every 3 bytes become 4 characters.
- **Percent-encoding**, usually called URL encoding: a byte that is not allowed in a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is written as `%` and two hex digits, so a space becomes `%20`. [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt) names it after the percent sign.

blocks.code:
import base64
from urllib.parse import quote, unquote

data = b"foo"
print(base64.b64encode(data))
print(base64.b64encode(b"f"), base64.b64encode(b"fo"))
print(base64.b64decode("Zm9v"))
print(data.hex(), bytes.fromhex("666f6f"))
print(quote("a b/c?d=1&e"), quote("a b/c?d=1&e", safe=""))
print(unquote("%24%7Bjndi%3A"))
blocks.caption: Output: `b'Zm9v'` / `b'Zg==' b'Zm8='` / `b'foo'` / `666f6f b'foo'` / `a%20b/c%3Fd%3D1%26e a%20b%2Fc%3Fd%3D1%26e` / `${jndi:`

blocks.title: Three bytes become four base64 characters

scenes.caption: The bytes f, o, o are 0x66, 0x6f, 0x6f in hex. Written as bits, that is 24 binary digits in groups of 8.
Base64 regroups the same 24 bits into four groups of 6. Each 6-bit group is a number from 0 to 63.
011001 is 25, 100110 is 38, 111101 is 61, 101111 is 47. In the base64 alphabet those are Z, m, 9 and v.
So foo encodes to Zm9v, 4 characters for 3 bytes. With only 1 or 2 bytes left over, = pads the end: f is Zg== and fo is Zm8=.

blocks.md: **Why attackers use encodings.** Not to hide from a determined analyst, since decoding takes one line, but to get past simple filters and to move binary data through text channels. MITRE ATT&CK lists standard encodings for command-and-control traffic as [T1132.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1132/001/), with many groups using base64. On Windows, PowerShell (Microsoft's command shell and scripting language, run as `pwsh` in current versions) has an `-EncodedCommand` parameter that accepts a script as base64; the [PowerShell docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_pwsh) say the encoded bytes must be UTF-16LE (two bytes per character, low byte first), which administrators use for awkward quoting and attackers use to keep commands out of plain sight in process logs. Decoding it for review is a daily analyst task:

blocks.code:
import base64

def decode_powershell(encoded):
    """Decode the text after pwsh -EncodedCommand for review."""
    raw = base64.b64decode(encoded, validate=True)
    return raw.decode("utf-16-le")

sample = "VwByAGkAdABlAC0ATwB1AHQAcAB1AHQAIAAnAGgAZQBsAGwAbwAnAA=="
print(decode_powershell(sample))
print(base64.b64decode(sample)[:8])
blocks.caption: Output: `Write-Output 'hello'` / `b'W\x00r\x00i\x00t\x00'`

blocks.md: The second line shows the raw bytes: a zero byte after every ASCII letter. That pattern is the fingerprint of UTF-16LE text. Decode it as UTF-8 instead and you get the right letters with an invisible null character between each pair, which breaks every search you run on it.

**URL encoding and Log4Shell.** In December 2021, CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) showed that the Java logging library Log4j would act on special lookup strings inside logged text, such as ones starting `${jndi:` (JNDI is the Java Naming and Directory Interface, Java's way of looking objects up on directory servers), so defenders scrambled to search web logs for the telltale lookup prefix. Cloudflare's [write-up](https://blog.cloudflare.com/exploitation-of-cve-2021-44228-before-public-disclosure-and-evolution-of-waf-evasion-patterns/) shows attackers quickly rewriting it with nested lookups so a plain text search would miss it. Encoding is the simplest version of the same trick: if a string arrives percent-encoded, perhaps twice, a search for the decoded form finds nothing. The defensive rule is to **decode before you match**:

blocks.caption: Output: `False` / `GET /?q=%24%7Bjndi%3A HTTP/1.1` / `True` / `http://www.iuqerfsodp9ifjaposdfjhgosurijfaewrwergwea.com`

blocks.title: Decoding until nothing changes

scenes.caption: The logged request was encoded twice: % itself became %25, so the dollar sign is %2524.
A direct search for the lookup prefix finds nothing. This is the miss a naive detector makes.
Round 1 of fully_unquote: %25 becomes %, so the text changes but is still encoded.
Round 2: %24, %7B and %3A become the dollar sign, the brace and the colon. The text changed again.
Round 3: unquote changes nothing, so the loop stops. max_rounds caps the work if someone sends a hundred layers.
Now the match succeeds. refang undoes the defanged form CISA used for the WannaCry domain so a tool can look it up.

blocks.md: **Defanging** is the habit of writing indicators so nobody clicks them by accident: `hxxp` for http, `[.]` for a dot, `[:]` for a colon. The CISA WannaCry alert writes the malware's hard-coded domain as `http[:]//www[.]iuqerfsodp9ifjaposdfjhgosurijfaewrwergwea.com`. Your tools should refang indicators when they load them and defang them again in anything a human will read, such as tickets and chat messages.

Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.
Encoding is reversible formatting, not secrecy. Normalize data (decode, lowercase, refang) before matching it, and expect attackers to stack encodings to slip past exact-match rules.

blocks.question: Which statement about base64 is true?
options: It encrypts data with a fixed key built into the standard
It compresses data so it fits in URLs
It makes data about one third larger, turning every 3 bytes into 4 characters
It can only encode text, not binary files
blocks.explain: Base64 carries 6 bits per character, so 24 bits (3 bytes) need 4 characters: roughly 33 percent growth. There is no key and no compression, and it was designed precisely for arbitrary binary data.

blocks.question: Your detection searches web logs for a known-bad string and has never fired, but a colleague finds the string percent-encoded twice in last week's logs. What is the best fix?
options: Add the twice-encoded form as a second exact string
Decode each field repeatedly until it stops changing, then search the decoded text
Search only for the % character
Base64-encode the logs first
blocks.explain: Adding encoded variants one by one never ends: once, twice, mixed case hex, partial encoding. Normalizing the input to a fixed point and matching once covers all of them, with a round limit so hostile input cannot make you loop forever.

lessons.title: HTTP and REST APIs: making requests safely

blocks.md:
Sooner or later a script needs to ask another system a question: is this address known to be malicious, who owns this domain, has this file been seen before? Those systems answer through an **API** (application programming interface: a documented way for one program to use another). Most security APIs speak **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), the same protocol your browser uses.

An HTTP exchange is one request and one response:

- The **request** has a method (`GET` to read, `POST` to send data), a URL, **headers** (name and value pairs such as an API key) and sometimes a body.
- The **response** has a numeric **status code**, headers and a body, usually JSON. Codes in the 200s mean success, 400s mean the client did something wrong (401 not authenticated, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), and 500s mean the server failed.

Many of these services call themselves **REST** APIs. REST (Representational State Transfer) is the name Roy Fielding, an editor of the HTTP standard, gave in a [2000 doctoral dissertation](https://ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm), to the architectural style behind the web: things are resources named by URLs, and clients transfer representations of them (today, mostly JSON). In practice "REST API" means: a URL per thing, HTTP methods to act on it, JSON in and out.

In Python the usual tool is [Requests](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/), a third-party library. Install it inside a **virtual environment** (a private folder of packages for one project): run `python3 -m venv .venv`, then `source .venv/bin/activate` (on Windows `.venv\Scripts\activate`), then `python3 -m pip install requests`. Many Linux and macOS systems refuse a plain `pip install`. Three habits make it safe for security tooling.

blocks.caption: A minimal, safe GET helper. Run without the variable set, it prints `set VT_API_KEY first` and exits with status 1.

blocks.md:
**1. Always set a timeout.** The Requests documentation is blunt: by default, requests do not time out, and without a timeout your code may hang for minutes or more. `timeout=(3.05, 10)` allows 3.05 seconds to connect and 10 seconds between bytes of the response. A hung enrichment job is a silent failure: alerts pile up unenriched and nothing reports an error.

**2. Check the status.** `r.raise_for_status()` raises `requests.HTTPError` for any 4xx or 5xx response. Without it, an error page becomes your "data", and `r.json()` either fails confusingly or returns an error object you then treat as a result.

**3. Keep TLS verification on.** HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS (Transport Layer Security), which encrypts the connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate. Requests verifies certificates by default. Passing `verify=False` to silence an error turns that proof off, so anyone on the network path could pose as the API and read your key.

blocks.title: Three things that can happen to one API call

scenes.caption: The script sends a GET for one file report, with the API key in the x-apikey header and a timeout set.
Normal case: 200 with a JSON body. raise_for_status does nothing and r.json() parses the body into dicts and lists.
The key is missing or wrong: the server answers 401. raise_for_status turns it into an HTTPError instead of letting an error body pass as data.
The server accepts the connection but never answers. With timeout=(3.05, 10) the script gets ReadTimeout after 10 quiet seconds; with no timeout it would wait indefinitely.

blocks.md: **Where the key lives.** An API key is a password for a program, so it must never be written in the code. Code gets committed, pasted into tickets and shared with colleagues. Instead, read it from an **environment variable**: a named value the operating system hands to every program it starts. You set `VT_API_KEY` in your shell or your scheduler's secret store, and `os.environ.get("VT_API_KEY")` reads it, returning `None` when it is missing so the script can stop with a clear message.

**Real case: Microsoft AI research, 2023.** Researchers at Wiz, a cloud security company, [found](https://www.wiz.io/blog/38-terabytes-of-private-data-accidentally-exposed-by-microsoft-ai-researchers) that a public Microsoft GitHub repository told readers to download AI models from an Azure Storage URL carrying a SAS (shared access signature) token. The token granted access to the entire storage account, not just the models, with full control rather than read-only rights, and was valid until 2051. Behind it sat 38 TB of private data, including workstation backups with secrets, passwords and over 30,000 internal Teams messages. A credential pasted into something public is exposed to everyone who reads it, however it is formatted.

Environment variables keep keys out of your code, not out of reach. Every process in the same environment can read them. In the Codecov compromise from lesson 7, the altered uploader sent CI environment variables, including credentials, tokens and keys, to the attacker, and Codecov told affected customers to re-roll all of them. Give each key the narrowest scope the service allows, never print it in logs, and rotate it when anything that could read it is compromised.

blocks.question: Your enrichment script calls `requests.get(url, headers=h)` with no timeout. One night the provider's load balancer accepts connections but stops answering. What happens?
options: Requests gives up after its default 30-second timeout
Python raises ConnectionError immediately
The operating system retries on another server
The call can wait indefinitely, so the job hangs and no error is reported
blocks.explain: Requests has no default timeout. A connection that is open but silent can block the call indefinitely, which in a scheduled job looks like "still running" rather than "failed". Always pass `timeout=`.

blocks.question: A teammate fixes a certificate error by adding `verify=False`. What did they actually change?
options: The script no longer checks that it is talking to the real server, so someone on the network path could impersonate the API and capture the key
Nothing important, the traffic is still encrypted so it is still safe
The request now uses plain HTTP
The API key is no longer sent
blocks.explain: Encryption without authentication protects you from nobody in particular: an attacker who intercepts the connection presents their own certificate, your script accepts it, and they read the key. Fix the trust problem (a missing corporate CA bundle, a wrong hostname) instead.

lessons.title: Enriching indicators: threat-intel lookups within rate limits

blocks.md:
**Enrichment** means adding context to a bare indicator before a human looks at it. An alert that says "file 5bef35..." is a puzzle; one that says "file 5bef35..., flagged malicious by many engines, first reported as the WannaCry dropper" is a decision. Analysts enrich all day, so it is the first thing teams automate.

The pattern is the same for every provider: validate the indicator, call the provider's API with your key, interpret the answer, respect the rate limit, cache what you learned. We use [VirusTotal](https://docs.virustotal.com/reference/file-info), a service that scans files with many antivirus engines and other tools, because its API is well documented.

What the VirusTotal v3 documentation specifies:

- A file report is `GET https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/files/{id}`, where `id` may be a SHA-256, SHA-1 or MD5 hash.
- Every request carries your key in the `x-apikey` header.
- The report's `data.attributes.last_analysis_stats` is a dict of counts such as `malicious`, `suspicious` and `undetected` from the latest scan.
- A hash it has never seen returns 404 with `NotFoundError`. Exceeding a quota returns 429 with `QuotaExceededError`.
- The free [Public API](https://docs.virustotal.com/reference/public-vs-premium-api) allows 500 requests per day and 4 per minute, and must not be used in commercial products or services, or in business workflows that do not contribute new files. At work you use your organization's licensed feed; the code pattern does not change.

**Rate limits** are how a service shares capacity: a fixed number of requests per minute or day per key. Status 429 Too Many Requests is defined in [RFC 6585](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585.txt), which says the response may include a `Retry-After` header telling you how long to wait. HTTP allows Retry-After to be a number of seconds or a date; the code below handles only seconds, and a date would raise ValueError in `int()`. A polite client paces itself so it rarely sees 429, and when it does, it waits and retries a bounded number of times instead of hammering the server or giving up on the whole batch.

blocks.caption: enrich.py: validate, look up, interpret, pace, cache.

blocks.title: One lookup that hits the rate limit and recovers

scenes.caption: First, the hash must look like an MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 in lowercase hex. Anything else never reaches the URL.
Attempt 0: the request goes out with the session's x-apikey header and a timeout.
The server answers 429. The code sleeps for Retry-After seconds (60 if the header is absent) and continue starts the next attempt.
Attempt 1: same request, now within quota.
200 this time. Neither the 404 nor the 429 branch runs, and raise_for_status passes.
Walk down the JSON to the stats dict and return a small summary. After max_tries failed attempts, the final line raises instead of looping forever.

blocks.title: Pacing five hashes at 4 requests per minute

scenes.caption: Simplified: each call is drawn as 1 s. After every lookup, enrich sleeps 60 / 4 = 15 s, so at most 4 calls start in any minute.
Hash 3 gets 429 anyway, perhaps because another script shares the key. The server says Retry-After: 30, so the code waits 30 s and retries.

Item 5 repeats hash 1 (in capitals). After normalizing it is already in the cache, so it costs no request and no sleep, and item 6 (hash 5) is looked up at once. The run ends at 111 s, after the last 15 s pace.

blocks.md: Tested against a local stand-in server (not VirusTotal) that answered with a made-up count, the input `5BEF35...` (capitals), the MD5 of the harmless notes.txt, then `5bef35...` again gave: known and malicious, `{'known': False}` for the harmless file, and the first result again from the cache with no third request. Passing `"../../users/me"` raised `ValueError: not an MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256` before any request was made.

A 404 means "this service has never seen the file", not "this file is safe". New or targeted malware is exactly what nobody has uploaded yet. Report unknown as unknown. Look up hashes rather than uploading files: VirusTotal's [How it works](https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/how-it-works) page says submitted files may be shared with its premium customers, so an upload can leak a confidential document or tip off an attacker.

blocks.prompt: Why does `lookup_hash` check the hash against a strict pattern before putting it into the URL, when the API would just return 404 for garbage anyway?
blocks.reveal: Because the string becomes part of a URL path, and you do not control where indicators come from: they arrive from alerts, emails and pasted tickets, some written by attackers. A value like `../../users/me` or one containing `?` or `#` changes which URL is requested, so your key could be sent to an endpoint you never meant to call. Validating with `fullmatch` on a strict allow-list pattern means only well-formed hashes can ever be sent. It also catches honest mistakes, like a hash with a trailing space, before they burn quota.

blocks.md: Every enrichment client needs the same five parts: strict input validation, a timeout, explicit handling of 404 and 429, a pace that respects the documented limit, and a cache so duplicates are free.

blocks.question: Your free-tier key allows 4 lookups per minute. A morning alert lists 600 unique hashes. With 15-second pacing and no 429s, roughly how long does enrichment take?
options: About 2.5 minutes
About 40 minutes
About 2.5 hours, and the free daily allowance of 500 runs out first anyway
About 15 seconds, because the requests run in parallel
blocks.explain: 600 lookups at 4 per minute is 150 minutes. The Public API also caps a key at 500 requests per day, so the last 100 would fail. This is the arithmetic that justifies a licensed feed, a local cache shared across runs, or deduplicating and prioritizing before you look anything up.

lessons.title: Turning a script into a command-line tool with argparse

blocks.md:
A script with the file name and threshold written inside it works for you, today. A **tool** takes its inputs from the command line, prints help, reports errors clearly and tells the caller how it went, so a teammate, a cron job or a SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) platform can run it without reading the code.

A **CLI** (command-line interface) passes your program a list of words called **arguments**: in `python3 authscan.py auth.log -t 3`, the arguments are `auth.log`, `-t` and `3`. Python's standard [argparse](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html) module (argument parser) turns that list into named values, checks their types and generates `--help` for free.

blocks.code:
import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

LINE = re.compile(
    r"(?P<result>Failed|Accepted) \S+ for (?:invalid user )?"
    r"(?P<user>\S+) from (?P<ip>\S+) port \d+ ssh2"
)

def scan(lines, threshold):
    failures = Counter()
    alerts = []
    for line in lines:
        m = LINE.search(line)
        if m is None:
            continue
        ip, user = m["ip"], m["user"]
        if m["result"] == "Failed":
            failures[ip] += 1
        elif failures[ip] >= threshold:
            alerts.append(f"{user} logged in from {ip} "
                          f"after {failures[ip]} failures")
    return failures, alerts

def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="authscan", description="Flag SSH logins after many failures.")
    p.add_argument("logfile", help="path to an sshd auth log")
    p.add_argument("-t", "--threshold", type=int, default=5,
                   help="failures before a success is suspicious")
    p.add_argument("--json", action="store_true", help="print JSON")
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        with open(args.logfile, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as f:
            failures, alerts = scan(f, args.threshold)
    except OSError as e:
        print(f"authscan: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if args.json:
        print(json.dumps({"failures": failures, "alerts": alerts}))
    else:
        for a in alerts:
            print("ALERT:", a)
    return 1 if alerts else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
blocks.caption: authscan.py: the parser from lesson 5 grown into a tool. It flags any successful login from an address that already failed at least threshold times.

blocks.md:
How the pieces fit:

- `add_argument("logfile")` is a **positional** argument: required, identified by position.
- `add_argument("-t", "--threshold", type=int, default=5)` is an **option**: optional, converted to an integer, 5 if absent. `-t five` is rejected with a usage message.
- `action="store_true"` makes `--json` a flag: present means `True`.
- `if __name__ == "__main__":` is true only when the file is run directly. When a test imports `authscan`, `__name__` is `"authscan"`, so `main()` does not run on import.
- `main(argv=None)` lets tests pass a list of arguments; `None` means "use the real command line".

blocks.title: scan() over three lines from auth.log
blocks.code:
import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter

LINE = re.compile(
    r"(?P<result>Failed|Accepted) \S+ for (?:invalid user )?"
    r"(?P<user>\S+) from (?P<ip>\S+) port \d+ ssh2"
)

def scan(lines, threshold):
    failures = Counter()
    alerts = []
    for line in lines:
        m = LINE.search(line)
        if m is None:
            continue
        ip, user = m["ip"], m["user"]
        if m["result"] == "Failed":
            failures[ip] += 1
        elif failures[ip] >= threshold:
            alerts.append(f"{user} logged in from {ip} "
                          f"after {failures[ip]} failures")
    return failures, alerts

scenes.caption: One pattern now covers both outcomes: the result group captures Failed or Accepted.
Line 4 of auth.log is an Invalid user line. It does not fit the pattern, so search returns None and the loop moves on.
Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.7: a failure, so the count for that address goes up.
Four more failures from the same address with other usernames bring the count to 5.
Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.7. Not a failure, so the elif checks 5 >= threshold (5): true, and an alert is recorded.

blocks.md:
**Exit codes** are how a program reports its result to whatever ran it: 0 means success and anything else means something to look at. authscan returns 0 for no alerts, 1 for alerts and 2 for an error, the same code argparse itself uses for bad arguments. A scheduler or SOAR playbook can branch on that number without parsing text.

The tool also separates its outputs. Results go to **stdout** (standard output); problems go to **stderr** (standard error) via `print(..., file=sys.stderr)`. If someone pipes the results into another program, error messages do not get mixed into the data. `--json` prints machine-readable output for the next tool in the chain.

blocks.code:
python3 authscan.py auth.log            # ALERT: deploy logged in from 203.0.113.7 after 5 failures   (exit 1)
python3 authscan.py auth.log -t 6       # no output   (exit 0)
python3 authscan.py auth.log --json     # {"failures": {"192.0.2.55": 3, "203.0.113.7": 5, "2001:db8::5": 1}, "alerts": [...]}
python3 authscan.py nope.log            # authscan: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'nope.log'   (stderr, exit 2)
python3 authscan.py auth.log -t five    # usage: authscan [-h] [-t THRESHOLD] [--json] logfile, then authscan: error: argument -t/--threshold: invalid int value: 'five'   (stderr, exit 2)
blocks.caption: Five runs against the sample log, with what each printed and its exit code.

blocks.title: Where each part of the tool's output goes

scenes.caption: The shell passes words, argparse turns them into typed values and hands them to scan.
Normal run: alerts go to stdout, where a person reads them or a pipe carries them on.
Problems go to stderr: a bad argument from argparse, or a missing file caught as OSError. The data stream stays clean.
The exit code travels back to the caller, which can open a ticket on 1 and page someone on 2.

blocks.md: Run `python3 authscan.py --help` and argparse prints the usage line, every argument and its help text. Writing good `help=` strings is the cheapest documentation you will ever produce.

blocks.question: authscan exits with code 2 when the log file is missing. A teammate suggests returning 0 instead, "since no alerts were found". Why is that a bad idea?
options: Exit code 0 is reserved for Windows
A scheduler would read 0 as a clean run, so a deleted or rotated log would look exactly like a quiet night
argparse will crash if main returns 0
It makes the JSON output invalid
blocks.explain: Exit codes are the contract with automation. "Could not check" must never look like "checked, nothing found", especially since attackers delete logs. Keep the error distinct and loud.

blocks.question: Why does the file end with `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())` instead of just `sys.exit(main())`?
options: So that importing authscan from a test runs no code and does not exit the test runner
It makes the script run faster
Because argparse requires it
So the script only works on Linux
blocks.explain: Importing a module runs its top-level code. Without the guard, `from authscan import scan` in a test file would parse the test runner's own arguments and call sys.exit. The guard is true only when the file is executed directly.

lessons.title: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code

blocks.md: Security scripts handle hostile input by design: log lines written by attackers, indicators pasted from phishing emails, fields from compromised hosts. Your tool can become the vulnerability. Three habits prevent most of it, and a scanner can check them for you.

**Habit 1: never eval data.** `eval(text)` (short for evaluate) runs `text` as Python code. The [built-in functions docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html) warn that it executes arbitrary code and that calling it with untrusted input leads to security vulnerabilities. People reach for it to turn `"[1, 2]"` or `"{'a': 1}"` into a value. Use the parser that matches the format instead: `json.loads` for JSON, and `ast.literal_eval` for Python literals, which accepts only strings, bytes, numbers, tuples, lists, dicts, sets, booleans, `None` and `Ellipsis`. The same applies to `pickle`: its docs state the module is not secure and that malicious pickle data can execute code during unpickling.

blocks.code:
import ast
import json

text = '{"threshold": 5, "allow": ["10.0.0.0/8"]}'
print(json.loads(text)["threshold"])
print(ast.literal_eval("[1, 'two', {'three': 3}]"))
try:
    ast.literal_eval("__import__('os').getcwd()")
except ValueError as e:
    print("refused:", type(e).__name__)
print(eval("__import__('os').getcwd()") == __import__("os").getcwd())
blocks.caption: Output: `5` / `[1, 'two', {'three': 3}]` / `refused: ValueError` / `True`. The last line shows eval happily running a function call that came in as text.

blocks.md: **Habit 2: run programs with a list, not a shell string.** `subprocess.run` starts another program. Given a list, it passes each item to the program as one argument, and the [subprocess docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html) note that because no shell is involved, shell metacharacters are passed through safely. Given a single string with `shell=True`, it hands the string to the system shell (`/bin/sh` on Unix), which treats `;`, `|`, `&&` and backticks as instructions. The docs put the burden on you: with `shell=True` it is the application's responsibility to quote everything correctly to avoid shell injection.

blocks.code:
import subprocess

host = "example.com; echo INJECTED"   # text from a ticket or alert

# Vulnerable: one string, handed to /bin/sh, which splits on ;
subprocess.run(f"echo checking {host}", shell=True)

# Fixed: a list is passed straight to the program as argv, no shell
subprocess.run(["echo", "checking", host])
blocks.caption: Output: `checking example.com` / `INJECTED` / `checking example.com; echo INJECTED`. The textbook illustration uses a harmless echo, but the shell would run any command in its place.

blocks.title: The same hostile text, through a shell and through a list

scenes.caption: The value came from an alert field, so the attacker chose it. It contains a semicolon.
Vulnerable: with shell=True the f-string becomes one command line, and the shell reads ; as the end of one command and the start of the next.
Fixed: the list goes straight to the program as argv. echo gets checking and the whole hostile string as one argument, and simply prints it. No shell ever sees the semicolon.

blocks.md: The list form stops shell injection, but the program you call may still misread an argument (for example one starting with `-`). So also validate inputs against what they should be. For an address, `ipaddress.ip_address` from the [ipaddress module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html) accepts only real IPv4 or IPv6 addresses:

blocks.caption: Output: `rejected: '192.0.2.1; echo INJECTED' does not appear to be an IPv4 or IPv6 address`. Note the timeout on the child process too.

blocks.md:
**Habit 3: keep secrets out of code and out of repositories.** Read keys from environment variables or a secret manager (lesson 9), keep local `.env` files listed in `.gitignore` so they are never committed, and when your code must create a token, use the `secrets` module, which its [docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/secrets.html) say should be used in preference to the default random number generator in the `random` module for anything security related.

**Let a tool check you.** [Bandit](https://bandit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) is a scanner for common security issues in Python code: it builds an AST (abstract syntax tree, the parsed structure of the program) from each file and runs checks against it. On a three-line file that uses `shell=True` and `eval`, it reported B602 (subprocess call with shell=True, severity High), B307 (use of possibly insecure function eval, suggesting `ast.literal_eval`, severity Medium) and B404 (a Low note that the subprocess module is imported). Install it with `python3 -m pip install bandit`, run `bandit -r .`, and add it to CI.
Data is never code. Parse it with a format-specific parser, pass it to other programs as list arguments, validate it against what it should be, and keep secrets in the environment, not in the file.

blocks.question: Which call is safe when `domain` comes from an alert?
options: subprocess.run(f"whois {domain}", shell=True)
subprocess.run("whois " + domain, shell=True)
os.system("whois " + domain)
subprocess.run(["whois", domain], timeout=30)
blocks.explain: Only the list form avoids the shell. The two shell=True strings and os.system all pass the text to /bin/sh, where a semicolon or backtick in domain starts a new command. Validating domain against a strict pattern is still a good second layer.

blocks.question: A colleague loads a config with `rules = eval(open("rules.txt").read())` because the file looks like a Python list. What should replace it?
options: exec instead of eval
pickle.loads
ast.literal_eval, or better, store the rules as JSON and use json.loads
eval with a try/except around it
blocks.explain: literal_eval accepts only literal values, so a function call in the file is refused with ValueError. JSON is even better because other tools can read it too. Wrapping eval in try/except does nothing: the injected code runs before any exception could happen, and pickle and exec have the same problem.

lessons.title: Testing your script so it does not fail silently

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 ended with a warning: security scripts fail by quietly counting the wrong thing. A **test** is a small piece of code that runs your code on input you chose and checks the answer you expect. When a test fails, you find out at your desk instead of during an incident.

Python ships a test framework, [unittest](https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html). Most teams use [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/getting-started.html), a third-party runner (`python3 -m pip install pytest` inside the virtual environment from lesson 9) with less ceremony: it finds files named `test_*.py`, runs every function whose name starts with `test`, and reports any `assert` (a statement that raises an error when its condition is false) that fails.

blocks.code:
from authscan import scan, main

FAIL = "sshd[1]: Failed password for {u} from {ip} port 2222 ssh2"
OK = "sshd[1]: Accepted password for {u} from {ip} port 2222 ssh2"

def test_success_after_many_failures_alerts():
    lines = [FAIL.format(u=f"user{i}", ip="203.0.113.7") for i in range(5)]
    lines.append(OK.format(u="deploy", ip="203.0.113.7"))
    failures, alerts = scan(lines, threshold=5)
    assert failures["203.0.113.7"] == 5
    assert alerts == ["deploy logged in from 203.0.113.7 after 5 failures"]

def test_below_threshold_is_quiet():
    lines = [FAIL.format(u="root", ip="192.0.2.55")] * 4
    lines.append(OK.format(u="root", ip="192.0.2.55"))
    assert scan(lines, threshold=5)[1] == []

def test_invalid_user_and_ipv6_are_counted():
    lines = [FAIL.format(u="invalid user oracle", ip="2001:db8::5")]
    failures, _ = scan(lines, threshold=5)
    assert failures == {"2001:db8::5": 1}

def test_missing_file_exits_2(capsys):
    assert main(["no-such.log"]) == 2
    assert "No such file" in capsys.readouterr().err
blocks.caption: test_authscan.py. Running `python3 -m pytest -q` prints `4 passed`.

blocks.prompt: Someone "simplifies" the pattern in authscan.py by deleting the `(?:invalid user )?` group. The script still runs without any error on the sample log. Which test fails, and what does a missed match mean in production?
blocks.reveal: `test_invalid_user_and_ipv6_are_counted` fails: `assert Counter() == {'2001:db8::5': 1}`, because without the optional group the word `invalid` is taken as the username and the pattern no longer fits, so nothing is counted. We ran exactly this change: `1 failed, 3 passed`. In production, attempts on usernames that do not exist (`admin`, `oracle`, `test`, the bulk of any stuffing run) would vanish from the counts, and the attack would sit below every threshold.

blocks.title: The broken pattern meets the test
blocks.code:
from authscan import scan, main

FAIL = "sshd[1]: Failed password for {u} from {ip} port 2222 ssh2"
OK = "sshd[1]: Accepted password for {u} from {ip} port 2222 ssh2"

def test_invalid_user_and_ipv6_are_counted():
    lines = [FAIL.format(u="invalid user oracle", ip="2001:db8::5")]
    failures, _ = scan(lines, threshold=5)
    assert failures == {"2001:db8::5": 1}

scenes.caption: The test builds one realistic line: a failed password for a username that does not exist, from an IPv6 address.
scan runs with the broken pattern. After for, it now expects the username then from, but the line continues invalid user oracle from, so search finds no match.
The assert compares the empty Counter with the expected count, fails, and pytest prints both sides so you see exactly what went wrong.

blocks.md: **Testing code that calls an API.** Tests must not touch the real service: they would be slow, spend quota, need a real key and fail whenever the network does. Because `lookup_hash` receives its session as a parameter, a test can pass a **fake**: a tiny class with a `get` method that returns prepared responses. pytest's `monkeypatch` fixture temporarily replaces `time.sleep` so the 429 test does not really wait.

blocks.caption: test_enrich.py. Running pytest prints `3 passed`, with no network access and no API key.

blocks.title: What the seven tests protect

scenes.caption: Tests per behaviour across both files. Each one encodes a mistake that would otherwise be silent: a missed format, a false alarm, a hidden error, a 404 read as clean, a hostile string in a URL.

blocks.md: Test the awkward inputs and the failure paths, not just the happy path, and keep tests offline with fakes. A test suite is what lets you change a detection script without wondering what you broke.

**Where to practise legally.** Use your own machine and data you are allowed to handle, or platforms built for practice:

- [picoCTF](https://picoctf.org/), Carnegie Mellon's free capture-the-flag platform, has General Skills and Forensics challenges where Python decoding, hashing and parsing are the whole job.
- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) offers defensive investigation challenges with real-looking logs and indicators to parse and enrich.
- The official [Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) fills in any language feature this course used only briefly.

A good first project: point authscan at a log from a lab virtual machine you own, add a per-username count, and write the tests before you change the pattern.

blocks.question: Why does test_enrich.py pass a FakeSession to lookup_hash instead of letting it call VirusTotal?
options: The real API does not support MD5
Tests should be fast, repeatable and offline: no quota, no key, and no failures caused by the network or by the service's data changing
pytest cannot import requests
Fakes make the code run in production too
blocks.explain: A test that depends on a live service fails for reasons unrelated to your code and spends real quota. Designing functions to receive their dependencies (here, the session) is what makes fakes possible.
